paragraphs: Once the legislative power is firmly established, the next task is to establish the executive power in the same way. The executive power works only through particular acts and is not part of the essence of the legislative power, so it is naturally separate from it. If the Sovereign, as such, could hold the executive power, right and fact would be so mixed up that no one could tell what was law and what was not. The body politic would be disfigured, and would soon fall victim to the very violence it was instituted to prevent.

By the social compact the citizens are all equal, so all can prescribe what all should do, but no one has the right to demand that another do what he does not do himself. This is exactly the right, indispensable for giving the body politic life and movement, that the Sovereign gives to the prince when it institutes the government.

Some have maintained that this act of establishment was a contract between the people and the rulers it sets over itself — a contract laying down conditions between the two parties, under which one is bound to command and the other to obey. Everyone will agree, I am sure, that this is a strange sort of contract to make. But let us see whether the view holds up.

First, the supreme authority can no more be altered than it can be transferred: limiting it destroys it. For the Sovereign to put a superior over itself is absurd and contradictory, and to bind itself to obey a master would mean returning to absolute liberty.
Moreover, such a contract between the people and certain persons would clearly be a particular act. It follows that it can be neither a law nor an act of Sovereignty, and so would be illegitimate.

It is plain, too, that in relation to each other the contracting parties would stand under the law of nature alone, with no guarantee at all of their mutual undertakings, which is wholly at odds with the civil state. Whoever commands force can always control how the contract is carried out. So it would come to the same thing to call it a “contract” when one man says to another, “I give you all my goods, on condition that you give me back as much of them as you please.”
There is only one contract in the State, and that is the act of association, which by itself rules out any second contract. No public contract can be conceived that would not violate the first.
